title: MODULE 03 — Java Backend Development with Spring Boot

overview.text: Module objective: Move from understanding backend architecture and designing APIs to implementing real backend applications using Java and Spring Boot.
In Module 01, you learned how backend systems are structured.
In Module 02, you learned how to design HTTP APIs and define their contracts.
Now, you will learn how to implement those concepts using Java and Spring Boot.
You will work with controllers, services, repositories, dependency injection, DTOs, entities, configuration, and application architecture.
The central project throughout this module will be a Student Management REST API.

By the end of this module, you should be able to build a working Java backend that receives HTTP requests, validates data, executes business logic, interacts with a database, and returns structured responses.

The course uses the current Spring Boot 4.2.0 documentation as its reference baseline (November 27, 2026). Spring Boot 4.2.0 requires Java 17 or later and supports Maven 3.6.3 or later. For this learning project, Java 21 is a suitable development target.

4.1 Why separate controllers, services, and repositories?
An administrator registers a new student.
Check whether the email address already exists.
Save the student to the database.
You could write all of this inside one controller method.
However, that would mix several responsibilities in a single location.
Instead, Spring Boot applications commonly use three layers:
Receives HTTP requests and returns responses
Executes business rules and coordinates operations
The controller is the entry point for HTTP requests.
It maps incoming requests to Java methods and returns appropriate HTTP responses.

@RestController @RequestMapping("/api/v1/students") public class StudentController { @GetMapping public String getStudents() { return "All students"; } @GetMapping("/{id}") public String getStudent(@PathVariable Long id) { return "Student ID: " + id; } }
Converts the request body into an object
The controller should not contain complicated business rules or direct database queries.
Its main job is to understand the HTTP request, invoke the appropriate application operation, and construct the HTTP response.
The service layer contains the application's business operations.
For example, when an administrator registers a student, the service should enforce rules such as:
Student registration must follow institute rules.
Student information must be saved correctly.

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service; @Service public class StudentService { public String registerStudent(String name, String email) { if (name == null || name.isBlank()) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( "Student name is required" ); } if (email == null || !email.contains("@")) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( "Valid email is required" ); } return "Student registered successfully"; } }
This is a simplified service without database persistence.
The service is independent of the HTTP request format.
The same operation could be invoked by:
This is one reason business logic should not be tightly coupled to controllers.
The repository is responsible for persistence operations.
It provides an interface through which the application can retrieve, store, update, and delete data.
public interface StudentRepository extends JpaRepository<Student, Long> { }
You do not need to manually implement standard CRUD operations.
Spring Data JPA provides an implementation through its repository infrastructure.
Spring Data can also derive database queries from repository method names.
Spring Data interprets the method name and generates an appropriate query implementation.
The layers communicate through Java method calls, not separate HTTP requests.
This is important: a three-layer monolithic application is not automatically a microservice architecture.
4.6 Why not put database code in the controller?
Consider a controller that directly executes a database operation:

@RestController public class StudentController { private final StudentRepository repository; public StudentController(StudentRepository repository) { this.repository = repository; } @PostMapping("/students") public Student createStudent( @RequestBody Student student) { return repository.save(student); } }
This may work for a small demonstration, but it has several problems:
Business rules become mixed with HTTP handling.
Multiple controllers may duplicate the same rules.
Data access concerns spread throughout the API.
The controller becomes harder to maintain.

@RestController public class StudentController { private final StudentService service; public StudentController(StudentService service) { this.service = service; } @PostMapping("/students") public StudentResponse createStudent( @RequestBody CreateStudentRequest request) { return service.createStudent(request); } }
The controller delegates the operation to the service.
Some responsibilities may be shared by additional components such as middleware, validators, and mappers, but the general boundaries should remain clear.
Fat controller: Too much application logic inside controller methods.
Anemic or meaningless service: A service that simply forwards every repository method without providing meaningful application behavior can add unnecessary abstraction.
Repository with business rules: Repositories should primarily handle persistence rather than application workflows.
Circular dependencies: For example, StudentService calls CourseService, while CourseService directly calls StudentService. This usually indicates poorly defined responsibilities.
Entity returned directly: Returning JPA entities from controllers can expose internal fields, relationships, or persistence details.

5. Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control
This is one of the fundamental concepts behind Spring Framework.
Understanding it will help you understand how Spring Boot manages application objects and connects components automatically.
Dependency Injection (DI) is a software design technique in which an object receives the other objects it depends on instead of creating or locating those objects itself.
Consider a student service that needs a repository.
public class StudentService { private StudentRepository repository = new StudentRepository(); }
There are several problems with this approach.
The service creates its own dependency.
The service is tightly coupled to a concrete implementation.
@Service public class StudentService { private final StudentRepository repository; public StudentService(StudentRepository repository) { this.repository = repository; } }
The service declares its dependency through the constructor.
Spring provides the dependency when it creates the service bean.
Inversion of Control (IoC) is a broader principle in which control over object creation or application flow is transferred from the application code to an external framework or container.
Application code | v Creates objects | v Connects dependencies | v Manages lifecycle
Spring Container | v Creates beans | v Resolves dependencies | v Connects objects | v Manages lifecycle
The application declares which components are needed.
The Spring container manages how those components are created and connected.
Dependency Injection is one way of implementing Inversion of Control.
A Spring Bean is an object created and managed by the Spring IoC container.
Several common annotations help register components.
Declares a managed object returned by a method
@Service, @Repository, and @Controller are specialized forms of Spring components.
They communicate the responsibility of a class and integrate with component scanning.
The Spring container is responsible for managing Spring Beans.
Makes beans available to other components.
A common Spring application context implementation is ApplicationContext.
You generally interact with Spring-managed objects through dependency injection rather than manually retrieving them from the context.
Constructor injection is generally the preferred approach for required dependencies.
@Service public class CourseService { private final CourseRepository repository; public CourseService(CourseRepository repository) { this.repository = repository; } }
Allows dependencies to be supplied without starting Spring.
For a class with one constructor, Spring can use that constructor without requiring an explicit @Autowired annotation.
Setter injection supplies a dependency through a setter method.

@Component public class ReportService { private NotificationService notificationService; @Autowired public void setNotificationService( NotificationService notificationService) { this.notificationService = notificationService; } }
This may be useful for optional or replaceable dependencies.
However, it allows the object to exist before the dependency is assigned. For required dependencies, constructor injection is usually clearer.
Field injection places the dependency directly into a field.
@Service public class StudentService { @Autowired private StudentRepository repository; }
Spring supports field injection, but it is generally less desirable for application design because:
The class may require reflection-based dependency setup.
Prefer constructor injection for required dependencies.
Suppose a platform sends a notification after a student registers.
public interface NotificationService { void sendWelcomeMessage(String email); }

@Service public class EmailNotificationService implements NotificationService { @Override public void sendWelcomeMessage(String email) { System.out.println( "Sending welcome message to " + email ); } }

@Service public class StudentService { private final NotificationService notificationService; public StudentService( NotificationService notificationService) { this.notificationService = notificationService; } public void registerStudent(String email) { // Save student here. notificationService.sendWelcomeMessage(email); } }
Spring discovers the notification service and injects it into the student service.
Notice that StudentService depends on the interface rather than directly constructing the email implementation.
This makes it possible to replace the notification provider without changing the business service's dependency declaration.
For example, later you could introduce an SMS or push notification implementation.
If multiple implementations are registered, Spring needs a way to determine which bean to inject. You can use @Qualifier or @Primary to make the selection explicit.
@Component: Placed on a class so that component scanning can discover it.

@Bean: Placed on a method inside a configuration class to explicitly register the returned object as a Spring Bean.
@Configuration public class ApplicationConfiguration { @Bean public Clock applicationClock() { return Clock.systemUTC(); } }
The Clock object becomes available for dependency injection.
@Bean is especially useful when registering third-party library classes that you cannot annotate with Spring's component annotations.
By default, Spring Beans are singleton-scoped within the application context.
This means Spring generally manages one shared bean instance for that definition.
Scope availability depends on the application environment.
For stateless services such as StudentService, singleton scope is generally suitable.
However, shared singleton services should not store user-specific request data in mutable instance fields. Doing so can cause concurrent requests to interfere with one another.
Suppose you want to test StudentService without connecting to a database.
You can provide a fake repository or a Mockito mock.

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) class StudentServiceTest { @Mock private StudentRepository repository; @InjectMocks private StudentService service; @Test void shouldFindStudent() { when(repository.existsByEmailIgnoreCase( "rahul@example.com" )).thenReturn(true); assertTrue( repository.existsByEmailIgnoreCase( "rahul@example.com" ) ); } }
This small example demonstrates repository mocking. A complete service test should exercise the service's own methods and verify their outcomes.
The key point is that dependencies can be supplied or replaced during tests without creating real infrastructure.
A useful design practice is that application logic should depend on abstractions where that improves flexibility and testing.
The service does not need to know how an email provider works.
This becomes particularly important when you study Clean Architecture and Hexagonal Architecture.

Spring MVC maps incoming HTTP requests to controller methods using annotations.
Can be handled by a Java method annotated with @GetMapping.
Used in Spring MVC applications, particularly when a method returns a view name or works with a web page.
Used for REST APIs. It combines @Controller and response-body behavior so that returned objects are written to the HTTP response body.
@RestController @RequestMapping("/api/v1/students") public class StudentController { @GetMapping public String getStudents() { return "Student data"; } }
In this REST controller, the returned string is the response body, not a template name.
Spring provides specialized request mapping annotations.

@RestController @RequestMapping("/api/v1/students") public class StudentController { @GetMapping public String findAll() { return "All students"; } @PostMapping public String create() { return "Student created"; } @GetMapping("/{id}") public String findOne(@PathVariable Long id) { return "Student ID: " + id; } @PutMapping("/{id}") public String replace(@PathVariable Long id) { return "Student replaced: " + id; } @PatchMapping("/{id}") public String update(@PathVariable Long id) { return "Student partially updated: " + id; } @DeleteMapping("/{id}") public String delete(@PathVariable Long id) { return "Student deleted: " + id; } }
These return strings for demonstration. Production endpoints should return appropriate response objects and HTTP status codes.
Path variables extract values from the URL.
@GetMapping("/{id}") public String getStudent(@PathVariable Long id) { return "Requested student: " + id; }
The value 101 is assigned to id.
@GetMapping("/{courseId}/modules/{moduleId}") public String getModule( @PathVariable Long courseId, @PathVariable Long moduleId) { return "Course: " + courseId + ", Module: " + moduleId; }
@GetMapping public String getStudents( @RequestParam(defaultValue = "1") int page, @RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") int pageSize) { return "Page: " + page + ", Page size: " + pageSize; }
You can mark an optional parameter using required = false.
@GetMapping("/search") public String searchStudents( @RequestParam(required = false) String department) { return "Department: " + department; }
The controller receives the query value.
@RequestBody converts the incoming request body into a Java object using an appropriate HTTP message converter.
public record CreateStudentRequest( String fullName, String email, String department ) {}
@PostMapping public String createStudent( @RequestBody CreateStudentRequest request) { return "Student: " + request.fullName(); }
Spring converts the JSON properties into the Java record fields.
Accepting data does not mean the data is valid.
The backend should reject invalid input.

import jakarta.validation.constraints.Email; import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank; import jakarta.validation.constraints.Size; public record CreateStudentRequest( @NotBlank @Size(max = 120) String fullName, @NotBlank @Email @Size(max = 255) String email, @Size(max = 80) String department ) {}
@PostMapping public String createStudent( @Valid @RequestBody CreateStudentRequest request) { return "Student accepted"; }
With the validation starter configured, Spring validates the request according to the constraints.
Invalid requests can produce a validation exception that is translated into an appropriate HTTP response.
Spring Boot provides integration with Jakarta Bean Validation through its validation support.
@PostMapping public ResponseEntity<String> createStudent() { return ResponseEntity .status(HttpStatus.CREATED) .body("Student created successfully"); }
@DeleteMapping("/{id}") public ResponseEntity<Void> deleteStudent( @PathVariable Long id) { // Delete student through the service. return ResponseEntity.noContent().build(); }

@RestController @RequestMapping("/api/v1/students") public class StudentController { private final StudentService studentService; public StudentController( StudentService studentService) { this.studentService = studentService; } @GetMapping("/{id}") public ResponseEntity<StudentResponse> getStudent( @PathVariable Long id) { StudentResponse response = studentService.getStudent(id); return ResponseEntity.ok(response); } }

This lesson covers an important backend design principle: the data stored in a database and the data exposed through an API should not automatically be the same structure.
An Entity represents a persistent object that is stored and managed by a persistence system, typically a relational database when using JPA.
For example, a Student entity may contain:

@Entity @Table(name = "students") public class Student { @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) private Long id; private String fullName; private String email; private String department; private String passwordHash; // Constructors, getters and setters }
The @Entity annotation identifies the class as a JPA entity.
The @Id annotation identifies its primary key.
@GeneratedValue specifies how the identifier is generated according to the configured strategy.
This entity represents the persistence model.
It is not necessarily the structure that should be returned to an API consumer.
DTO stands for Data Transfer Object.
A DTO is an object used to transfer information between application boundaries.
In a Spring Boot REST API, DTOs are commonly used to represent incoming request data and outgoing response data.
public record StudentResponse( Long id, String fullName, String email, String department ) {}
This response contains only the information that the frontend needs.
It does not expose the password hash or internal persistence details.
7.4 Why should entities not be returned directly?
@Entity public class Student { @Id @GeneratedValue private Long id; private String fullName; private String email; private String passwordHash; private String internalNotes; }
A developer might return the entity directly:
@GetMapping("/{id}") public Student getStudent(@PathVariable Long id) { return repository.findById(id).orElseThrow(); }
Sensitive fields might be exposed in the API response.
The API becomes dependent on the database entity structure.
JPA relationships may contain lazy-loaded objects or bidirectional relationships that cause unexpected serialization behavior or recursion.
A database change can unintentionally change the API response.
If incoming request data is bound directly to entities, clients may attempt to set fields that they should never control, such as administrative flags or account permissions.
Separating entities and DTOs helps prevent these problems.
It is common to create separate request and response DTOs.
public record CreateStudentRequest( @NotBlank String fullName, @NotBlank @Email String email, @NotBlank String department ) {}
This defines what the client may submit when creating a student.
public record UpdateStudentRequest( @NotBlank String fullName, @NotBlank @Email String email, @NotBlank String department ) {}
This defines what the client may provide when updating a student.
public record StudentResponse( Long id, String fullName, String email, String department ) {}
This defines what the API returns.
The request and response structures need not be identical.
The application needs to convert that entity into a response DTO.

public class StudentMapper { public StudentResponse toResponse(Student student) { return new StudentResponse( student.getId(), student.getFullName(), student.getEmail(), student.getDepartment() ); } }
The service can use this mapper:
public StudentResponse getStudent(Long id) { Student student = repository.findById(id) .orElseThrow(() -> new StudentNotFoundException(id) ); return mapper.toResponse(student); }
The frontend receives the DTO, not the complete database entity.
7.7 Why different operations need different DTOs
Might additionally include account status and registration date.
A separate DTO for each operation makes these contracts explicit.
Developer writes the conversion code directly.
Advantages: Simple, transparent, and suitable for small projects.
Create dedicated classes to handle transformations.
Advantages: Reusable and keeps services smaller.
A Java annotation processor that generates mapper implementations at compile time.
Useful when an application contains many DTOs and complex conversions.
The important thing is to ensure that data is transformed intentionally, rather than exposing all entity properties automatically.
DTOs are also useful for request validation.
public record CreateCourseRequest( @NotBlank @Size(min = 3, max = 150) String title, @NotBlank String description, @NotNull Difficulty difficulty ) {}
The request describes exactly which values the client may submit and which validation rules apply.
An enum can restrict the difficulty value:
public enum Difficulty { BEGINNER, INTERMEDIATE, ADVANCED }
The backend can then reject unsupported values during request conversion or validation.
A course response may contain a summary of its modules.
public record CourseResponse( Long id, String title, List<ModuleSummary> modules ) { public record ModuleSummary( Long id, String title, int lessonCount ) {} }
This response structure presents the information required by the frontend without exposing the complete database relationship graph.
For large course content, you may return module summaries and expose a separate endpoint to retrieve individual module information.
The entity contains a password hash field for persistence demonstration.
No password-related field appears in the response DTO.
Why should entities and DTOs be separated?
What is the difference between request and response DTOs?
Why can returning entities directly create serialization problems?
What is the purpose of a mapper?
8.1 Why does a backend need configuration?
A backend application needs different settings depending on where it runs.
During local development, it may use:
Database: Local H2 Port: 8080 Logging: Detailed Environment: Development
Database: Managed PostgreSQL Port: Platform-configured Logging: Structured Environment: Production
Should developers change Java source code every time the environment changes?
Application configuration separates environment-specific values from business logic.
Spring Boot supports application configuration using properties files or YAML files.
spring: application: name: student-management datasource: url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/students username: student_user password: ${DB_PASSWORD} server: port: 8080
YAML uses indentation to establish nested configuration structure.
If the database URL is hardcoded in Java classes, deployment becomes difficult.
Instead, application code reads configuration from the environment.
This allows the same application binary to run in different environments.
Environment variables are values supplied to a process by its execution environment.
Spring Boot can resolve environment variables as configuration properties.
spring: datasource: url: ${DB_URL} username: ${DB_USERNAME} password: ${DB_PASSWORD} server: port: ${PORT:8080}
means use the supplied PORT value when available; otherwise use 8080.
Example local environment configuration on Linux or macOS:
export DB_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/students export DB_USERNAME=student_user export DB_PASSWORD=local_password mvn spring-boot:run
A profile allows an application to use environment-specific configuration.
spring: jpa: show-sql: true logging: level: com.example.studentmanagement: DEBUG
spring: jpa: show-sql: false logging: level: root: INFO
Or specify the active profile through configuration:
Production deployments often activate the profile through environment variables or deployment configuration rather than committing an environment-specific production selection into the application.
Spring Boot supports configuration from multiple sources, including:
Higher-priority configuration sources can override lower-priority values.
For example, an application may define:
But the deployment environment may provide:
The external configuration can override the default port setting.
This helps the application adapt to deployment infrastructure without modifying its source code.
The password may be committed to Git, exposed in code reviews, or unintentionally included in a distributed artifact.
Instead, use externalized configuration and a suitable secret management solution.
Remember that environment variables are not automatically safe against every form of host or process-level access. Production systems should use an appropriate secrets-management strategy.
For larger configuration groups, using individual @Value annotations everywhere can become difficult to maintain.
Spring Boot provides @ConfigurationProperties for structured configuration binding.

import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties; @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.course") public record CourseProperties( int defaultPageSize, int maximumPageSize ) {}

@SpringBootApplication @ConfigurationPropertiesScan public class StudentManagementApplication { public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run( StudentManagementApplication.class, args ); } }
Inject the configuration into a service:
@Service public class CourseService { private final CourseProperties properties; public CourseService(CourseProperties properties) { this.properties = properties; } }
Now the application has a structured and type-safe configuration object.
You can also use validation on configuration properties where appropriate.
spring: datasource: url: ${DB_URL} username: ${DB_USERNAME} password: ${DB_PASSWORD} jpa: hibernate: ddl-auto: validate show-sql: false properties: hibernate: format_sql: true
ddl-auto: validate checks the database schema against the entity mappings rather than automatically modifying the schema.
Other modes include create, create-drop, and update, but these should be chosen carefully.
For production database schema management, versioned migration tools such as Flyway or Liquibase are generally preferable to relying on automatic schema updates.
Using different database schemas without understanding them.
Activating a test profile in a production deployment.
Hardcoding URLs and ports in Java classes.
Assuming local configuration is identical to cloud configuration.
Using database auto-update settings carelessly in production.
spring: application: name: student-management server: port: 8080
Run the application under both profiles and verify that the configuration changes work.
Why should database credentials not be hardcoded?
How can an external setting override an application YAML value?
Why is ddl-auto: update not a complete production migration strategy?
A service is reusable when it provides a clearly defined application capability that can be used by multiple parts of the application without duplicating its business rules.
If each module independently implements student retrieval and validation, the application will contain duplicated logic.
A reusable service provides a shared operation.
Imagine three modules need to retrieve a student.
If the business requirement changes, developers may have to update all three locations.
Instead, create a clearly defined service operation.

@Service public class StudentService { private final StudentRepository repository; public StudentService(StudentRepository repository) { this.repository = repository; } public Student findStudentById(Long id) { return repository.findById(id) .orElseThrow(() -> new StudentNotFoundException(id) ); } }
Other application services can use this operation where appropriate.
However, avoid turning one service into a massive shared utility that every module depends on. Services should have cohesive responsibilities.
A well-designed application service may be responsible for:
Converting domain outcomes into application responses.
For example, course enrollment may require:
Verify that the course is published.
Check that the student is eligible.
This belongs in an enrollment operation rather than in the HTTP controller.

@Service public class EnrollmentService { private final StudentRepository studentRepository; private final CourseRepository courseRepository; private final EnrollmentRepository enrollmentRepository; public EnrollmentService( StudentRepository studentRepository, CourseRepository courseRepository, EnrollmentRepository enrollmentRepository) { this.studentRepository = studentRepository; this.courseRepository = courseRepository; this.enrollmentRepository = enrollmentRepository; } @Transactional public Enrollment enroll(Long studentId, Long courseId) { Student student = studentRepository.findById(studentId) .orElseThrow(() -> new StudentNotFoundException(studentId) ); Course course = courseRepository.findById(courseId) .orElseThrow(() -> new CourseNotFoundException(courseId) ); if (!course.isPublished()) { throw new IllegalStateException( "Course is not available" ); } if (enrollmentRepository .existsByStudentIdAndCourseId(studentId, courseId)) { throw new IllegalStateException( "Student is already enrolled" ); } Enrollment enrollment = new Enrollment(student, course); return enrollmentRepository.save(enrollment); } }
This is illustrative and assumes that the corresponding entities, repositories, constructors, and database constraints have been implemented.
Notice how the enrollment process coordinates several objects.
A controller should not need to know these internal steps.
9.6 Understanding service reuse vs code duplication
There are two important forms of reuse.
Method-level reuse: The same operation is used in several application flows.
Component-level reuse: A shared capability, such as email notification, is provided through a common interface and implementation.
public interface NotificationService { void send(String recipient, String message); }
Different implementations can provide email, SMS, or push notification delivery.
This makes application features less dependent on specific external providers.
Database operations often need to be treated as one logical unit.
Without a properly designed transaction boundary, earlier changes may remain committed while the operation is only partially completed.
@Transactional allows Spring to manage the transaction around an application operation.

@Service public class EnrollmentService { @Transactional public Enrollment enrollStudent( Long studentId, Long courseId) { // Validate. // Save enrollment. // Update related database state. return null; } }
The transaction normally commits if the operation completes successfully and rolls back for applicable failures.
Spring's default rollback rules distinguish unchecked and checked exceptions, and these rules can be configured.
Use transactions around coherent business operations rather than placing @Transactional everywhere without understanding the boundary.
For operations that only retrieve information:
@Transactional(readOnly = true) public Student findStudent(Long id) { return repository.findById(id) .orElseThrow(); }
The readOnly flag communicates the intended transaction behavior and may allow persistence providers or transaction infrastructure to optimize the operation.
It should not be treated as a universal hard security guarantee that writes are impossible.
StudentService ├── Register student ├── Manage courses ├── Create assignments ├── Process payments ├── Send emails ├── Calculate progress ├── Generate reports └── Manage attendance
This is a poor organization because unrelated business capabilities are combined.
StudentService CourseService EnrollmentService AssignmentService AttendanceService ProgressService NotificationService ReportService
Each service should have a clear responsibility.
Suppose EnrollmentService depends on three repositories.
You can test enrollment rules by mocking those repositories and verifying:
This lets developers test the business rules without running a complete production environment.
Create a StudentManagement backend with these services:
Write at least one unit test for each important business service.
Why should business rules not be duplicated across modules?
Why should service classes have cohesive responsibilities?
How does dependency injection support service reuse?
Why should database transaction boundaries generally follow business operations?
Layered architecture is a software design approach that separates an application into logical layers, where each layer has a distinct responsibility.
In Spring Boot, a common organization is:
This is the architecture introduced in Module 01, now implemented using actual Java and Spring components.
Spring MVC Controllers · Request DTOs · Response DTOs
Understands HTTP and translates requests into application operations.
Coordinates business operations and enforces application rules.
Spring Data JPA · Repositories · Entity mapping
Handles database access and persistence operations.
The presentation layer handles external communication.
In a Spring Boot REST API, this commonly consists of:

@RestController @RequestMapping("/api/v1/students") public class StudentController { private final StudentService studentService; public StudentController(StudentService studentService) { this.studentService = studentService; } @GetMapping("/{id}") public ResponseEntity<StudentResponse> getStudent( @PathVariable Long id) { return ResponseEntity.ok( studentService.getStudent(id) ); } }
The controller handles HTTP communication and delegates the actual operation.
For example, a student enrollment operation may require several steps:
Enrollment Operation | v Find Student | v Find Course | v Check Eligibility | v Check Duplicate Enrollment | v Save Enrollment | v Return Result
The service layer ensures that the operation follows the application's rules.
The persistence layer communicates with the database.
public interface StudentRepository extends JpaRepository<Student, Long> { boolean existsByEmailIgnoreCase(String email); }
Spring Data JPA generates the implementation of the repository interface.

@Service public class StudentService { private final StudentRepository repository; public StudentService(StudentRepository repository) { this.repository = repository; } public boolean emailExists(String email) { return repository.existsByEmailIgnoreCase(email); } }
The database stores the actual records.
CREATE TABLE students ( id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, full_name VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL, email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL, department VARCHAR(80) );
The JPA entity maps Java objects to database records.
The application uses the repository and persistence provider to communicate with the database.
In a traditional layered architecture, dependencies generally flow from higher application layers to lower infrastructure layers.
Controller | v Service | v Repository | v Database
The controller should not bypass the service and directly manipulate persistence data unless there is a deliberate design reason.
Likewise, repositories should not depend on controllers.
A clean separation prevents unrelated components from becoming tightly coupled.
Separation of concerns: Each layer has a defined responsibility.
Maintainability: Changes in one layer are less likely to require changes everywhere.
Testability: Controllers, services, and repositories can be tested separately.
Reusability: Application services can be used by different entry points.
Team organization: Developers can work on specific parts of the application.
Simplified debugging: The request-processing flow is easier to trace.
Unnecessary pass-through methods: A service that only forwards every call to a repository without adding meaningful behavior can create unnecessary code.
Large service classes: Poorly divided services may accumulate unrelated business responsibilities.
Database coupling: In traditional layered systems, application services may depend closely on database-oriented repository interfaces.
Too many abstractions: Creating interfaces for every class, even when they provide no real benefit, can increase complexity.
A good layered architecture should be clear and appropriately sized, not artificially complicated.
It is important to understand that layered architecture is about code organization, not necessarily deployment.
You can have a modular monolithic backend that contains several layers.

Spring Boot Application │ ├── Student Module │ ├── Controller │ ├── Service │ └── Repository │ ├── Course Module │ ├── Controller │ ├── Service │ └── Repository │ ├── Enrollment Module │ ├── Controller │ ├── Service │ └── Repository │ └── Shared Infrastructure ├── Configuration └── Exception Handling
Everything can still run inside one Spring Boot application.
This is a suitable organization for many initial production systems.
10.11 When should you use layered architecture?
Maintaining a small or medium-sized backend.
Separating HTTP, business logic, and persistence concerns.
Supporting multiple developers working on different layers.

Which layer should contain HTTP request handling?
Where should business rules be implemented?

Why should repositories not depend on controllers?
Can layered architecture be used inside a monolithic application?
What problems can arise from excessive abstraction?

sections.title: 11. Introduction to Clean and Hexagonal Architecture

blocks.text: As applications become more complicated, the traditional layered approach may not provide enough separation between business rules and infrastructure.
This lesson introduces two important architecture styles that help manage this complexity.
11.1 Why do applications need stronger architectural boundaries?
Imagine a Student Management application that uses:
An external email provider for notifications.
A third-party storage service for student documents.
Over time, the application becomes strongly connected to these technologies.
Suppose you want to replace PostgreSQL with a different storage mechanism.
Or add a new way to execute business operations that does not come through HTTP.
If critical business rules are tightly coupled to infrastructure code, these changes can become difficult.
Clean and Hexagonal Architecture aim to reduce this dependence.
Clean Architecture is an architectural approach that separates important business rules from external technologies.
Business logic should not depend directly on frameworks, databases, or user interface technologies.
A conceptual structure looks like this:
External Systems Web / Database / Email | v Interface Adapters Controllers / Gateways | v Application Use Cases | v Domain Entities
The innermost components represent the most important business concepts.
External components depend on those inner concepts rather than requiring them to depend on specific technologies.
Domain entities represent important business concepts.
An entity may contain business behavior.

public class Enrollment { private final Long studentId; private final Long courseId; private boolean active; public Enrollment(Long studentId, Long courseId) { this.studentId = studentId; this.courseId = courseId; this.active = true; } public void cancel() { this.active = false; } public boolean isActive() { return active; } }
This example demonstrates a simple domain object.
It does not need to know about HTTP requests or a particular database implementation.
A use case represents an application operation.
A use case coordinates the domain behavior needed to accomplish an application goal.
EnrollStudentUseCase | v Load Student | v Load Course | v Validate Enrollment | v Create Enrollment | v Save Enrollment
The use case should focus on what the application needs to accomplish, not how HTTP or SQL works.
Interface adapters translate information between external systems and the application's internal model.
REST controllers translate HTTP requests into application inputs.
Response presenters translate outcomes into API response DTOs.
Database adapters convert between persistence entities and domain objects.
External API adapters communicate with third-party providers.
The external layer contains implementation technologies, such as:
These components support the application but should not own its most important business rules.
Hexagonal Architecture is also known as Ports and Adapters Architecture.
It organizes an application around its core business logic and defines explicit interfaces, called ports, through which external systems interact.
A port defines what the application needs.
An adapter provides a particular implementation of that requirement.
Domain rules · Use cases · Business operations
The hexagon is simply a conceptual drawing convention. It does not mean an application needs exactly six components or six interfaces.
A port is an interface that represents a communication boundary.
For example, suppose the application needs to save students.
public interface StudentRepositoryPort { Student save(Student student); Optional<Student> findById(Long id); }
The application core depends on the interface.
It does not depend on PostgreSQL or Spring Data JPA directly.
An adapter implements a port using a specific technology.

@Repository public class JpaStudentRepositoryAdapter implements StudentRepositoryPort { private final SpringDataStudentRepository repository; public JpaStudentRepositoryAdapter( SpringDataStudentRepository repository) { this.repository = repository; } @Override public Student save(Student student) { // Convert domain object into JPA entity. // Persist using Spring Data JPA. // Convert back to domain object. return student; } @Override public Optional<Student> findById(Long id) { return repository.findById(id) .map(this::toDomain); } private Student toDomain(StudentEntity entity) { // Mapping implementation. return new Student(entity.getFullName()); } }
This is an illustrative adapter; a real implementation requires complete entity and domain mapping.
The adapter connects the domain's persistence requirement to a particular database implementation.
Ports can be understood through two broad groups.
Describe operations that the outside world can invoke on the application.
Describe external capabilities required by the application.
Inbound adapters invoke the inbound ports.
Outbound adapters implement the outbound ports.
11.11 Traditional layered vs Clean vs Hexagonal
Protect business rules using dependency boundaries
Connect the core through ports and adapters
For example, an application may use layered organization inside individual modules while applying Hexagonal Architecture to modules with complicated external integrations.
11.12 When is Clean or Hexagonal Architecture useful?
Multiple database or external provider implementations may be needed.
The application has many integration points.
Automated business-logic testing is a priority.
Framework or infrastructure changes should not require rewriting core rules.
Multiple interfaces need to invoke the same application capabilities.
However, not every CRUD project needs full Clean Architecture.
For a small application with straightforward persistence and few integrations, traditional layered architecture may be more appropriate.
A good engineer selects the minimum architectural complexity that meets the actual requirements.
Take the student registration feature and redesign it using Ports and Adapters.
Explain which components belong to the business core and which belong to infrastructure.
Why should business logic not depend directly on PostgreSQL or Spring MVC?
When would ordinary layered architecture be enough?

sections.title: 12. Building and Organizing a Maintainable Backend

blocks.text: The final lesson brings all the previous concepts together.
A working backend is not automatically a maintainable backend.
An application may work today but become difficult to extend, test, debug, and operate as the number of features increases.
Professional backend development requires deliberate decisions about code organization, reliability, testing, configuration, and long-term maintenance.
Backend ├── MainController.java ├── AllService.java ├── Database.java ├── Helpers.java └── Everything.java
Backend ├── StudentModule ├── CourseModule ├── EnrollmentModule ├── AssignmentModule ├── Common └── Configuration
The second organization makes it easier to identify responsibilities and evolve features independently.
For a growing modular monolith, a package-by-feature structure is often a practical starting point.

com.example.learningplatform/ │ ├── LearningPlatformApplication.java │ ├── student/ │ ├── api/ │ ├── application/ │ ├── domain/ │ └── infrastructure/ │ ├── course/ │ ├── api/ │ ├── application/ │ ├── domain/ │ └── infrastructure/ │ ├── enrollment/ │ ├── api/ │ ├── application/ │ ├── domain/ │ └── infrastructure/ │ ├── assignment/ │ ├── api/ │ ├── application/ │ ├── domain/ │ └── infrastructure/ │ └── common/ ├── exception/ ├── configuration/ └── utilities/
This structure combines feature grouping with internal technical boundaries.
Each feature can be understood and maintained without searching through every unrelated class in the entire project.
Avoid putting complex database operations, email processing, enrollment calculations, or large business workflows directly inside controller methods.
A service should represent a meaningful application capability.
It should not become the place for every operation in the system.
If a service grows too large, review whether its responsibilities should be split into separate use cases or components.
If every controller constructs errors differently, frontend developers will need to handle many different response structures.
A centralized exception-handling mechanism provides consistency.

@RestControllerAdvice public class GlobalExceptionHandler { @ExceptionHandler(StudentNotFoundException.class) public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handleNotFound( StudentNotFoundException exception) { ApiError error = new ApiError( "STUDENT_NOT_FOUND", exception.getMessage() ); return ResponseEntity .status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND) .body(error); } }
public record ApiError( String code, String message ) {}
This ensures that missing-student errors are handled consistently throughout the application.
A complete implementation should also handle request validation failures, duplicate records, authentication failures, and unexpected exceptions.
Do not expose stack traces or sensitive infrastructure details to API clients.
Validate untrusted input at system boundaries.
public record RegisterStudentRequest( @NotBlank @Size(max = 120) String fullName, @NotBlank @Email String email, @NotBlank String department ) {}
The validation layer should check input format and constraints.
The service should enforce business rules.
These are related but different responsibilities.
A service checks whether a student is allowed to register.
A database unique constraint protects uniqueness at persistence level.
Validation at multiple relevant boundaries helps prevent invalid or inconsistent data.
Suppose a student enrolls in a course.
Use a transaction when those database operations need to succeed or fail as one unit.
However, do not hold an ordinary database transaction open while waiting for a lengthy external API or email operation.
For complex workflows, consider transactionally storing an event or outbox record and processing the external operation separately.
A maintainable backend needs more than manually testing each endpoint in Postman.
Spring Boot supports JUnit-based testing and integration with common testing libraries through its test dependencies.
12.9 Test business rules with unit tests

class EnrollmentRulesTest { @Test void duplicateEnrollmentShouldBeRejected() { // Arrange: // Create an existing enrollment. // Act: // Attempt the same enrollment again. // Assert: // Verify that the operation is rejected. } }
This is a test-design outline. In the practical lab, you will implement executable tests using JUnit and Mockito.
For example, creating a student with valid information should return 201 rather than a generic 200 if your API contract defines resource creation that way.
Logs help developers investigate what happens inside a backend.
Do not log passwords, access tokens, private documents, or unnecessary personal information.
Use a request or correlation ID to connect related log entries across an operation.
A maintainable application should expose operational information.
Spring Boot Actuator provides production-oriented endpoints for health, metrics, and application management.
With the appropriate dependency, you can expose a health endpoint, commonly:
Actual details depend on the application's Actuator configuration and enabled health indicators.
Management endpoints must be secured and should not expose sensitive information publicly.
A backend database schema changes as features evolve.
students - id - full_name - email - department - created_at
Instead of relying on automatic schema modification in production, use controlled database migrations.
Tools such as Flyway and Liquibase allow schema changes to be tracked and applied in a defined order.
ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN department VARCHAR(80);
Each migration should be version-controlled, reviewed, and tested.
A new developer should be able to understand how to start the application and where to find its important components.
A few useful software engineering principles:
Single Responsibility Principle: A class should have one cohesive responsibility.
Open/Closed Principle: Software components should be designed so that suitable extensions can be introduced without repeatedly modifying stable existing behavior.
Dependency Inversion Principle: High-level business logic should not depend directly on low-level implementation details when abstraction is appropriate.
DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself): Avoid duplicated business logic.
KISS (Keep It Simple): Prefer the simplest design that satisfies the requirements.
YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It): Avoid building complexity for requirements that have not materialized.
These principles support maintainable backend development, but they should be applied thoughtfully rather than mechanically.
Consider the architecture of a student management backend after completing this module.
This design demonstrates the relationship between HTTP handling, application logic, persistence, and external integrations.
It is a foundation that can be expanded as the application develops.

Build a functioning backend application using:

Part A — Define the application requirements

Part C — Understand the final project structure

student-api/ │ ├── pom.xml │ └── src/ │ ├── main/ │ │ │ ├── java/ │ │ └── com/example/studentapi/ │ │ │ │ │ ├── StudentApiApplication.java │ │ │ │ │ ├── student/ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ├── controller/ │ │ │ │ └── StudentController.java │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ├── service/ │ │ │ │ └── StudentService.java │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ├── repository/ │ │ │ │ └── StudentRepository.java │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ├── entity/ │ │ │ │ └── Student.java │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └── dto/ │ │ │ ├── CreateStudentRequest.java │ │ │ ├── UpdateStudentRequest.java │ │ │ └── StudentResponse.java │ │ │ │ │ └── common/ │ │ └── exception/ │ │ ├── StudentNotFoundException.java │ │ ├── DuplicateEmailException.java │ │ ├── ApiError.java │ │ └── GlobalExceptionHandler.java │ │ │ └── resources/ │ └── application.yml │ └── test/ └── java/

Spring Boot's dependency management supplies compatible versions for managed dependencies, so individual versions are not needed for the dependencies above.
Part E — Create the main application class

package com.example.studentapi; import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication; import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication; @SpringBootApplication public class StudentApiApplication { public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run( StudentApiApplication.class, args ); } }
This is the entry point of the entire application.

package com.example.studentapi.student.service; import com.example.studentapi.common.exception.DuplicateEmailException; import com.example.studentapi.common.exception.StudentNotFoundException; import com.example.studentapi.student.dto.CreateStudentRequest; import com.example.studentapi.student.dto.UpdateStudentRequest; import com.example.studentapi.student.dto.StudentResponse; import com.example.studentapi.student.entity.Student; import com.example.studentapi.student.repository.StudentRepository; import org.springframework.stereotype.Service; import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional; import java.util.List; import java.util.Locale; @Service public class StudentService { private final StudentRepository repository; public StudentService(StudentRepository repository) { this.repository = repository; } @Transactional public StudentResponse createStudent( CreateStudentRequest request) { String email = normalizeEmail(request.email()); if (repository.existsByEmailIgnoreCase(email)) { throw new DuplicateEmailException(email); } Student student = new Student( request.fullName().trim(), email, request.department().trim() ); Student saved = repository.save(student); return toResponse(saved); } @Transactional(readOnly = true) public List<StudentResponse> getAllStudents() { return repository.findAll() .stream() .map(this::toResponse) .toList(); } @Transactional(readOnly = true) public StudentResponse getStudentById(Long id) { Student student = findEntityById(id); return toResponse(student); } @Transactional public StudentResponse updateStudent( Long id, UpdateStudentRequest request) { Student student = findEntityById(id); String email = normalizeEmail(request.email()); if (!student.getEmail().equalsIgnoreCase(email) && repository.existsByEmailIgnoreCase(email)) { throw new DuplicateEmailException(email); } student.setFullName(request.fullName().trim()); student.setEmail(email); student.setDepartment(request.department().trim()); Student updated = repository.save(student); return toResponse(updated); } @Transactional public void deleteStudent(Long id) { Student student = findEntityById(id); repository.delete(student); } private Student findEntityById(Long id) { return repository.findById(id) .orElseThrow(() -> new StudentNotFoundException(id) ); } private String normalizeEmail(String email) { return email.trim().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT); } private StudentResponse toResponse(Student student) { return new StudentResponse( student.getId(), student.getFullName(), student.getEmail(), student.getDepartment() ); } }
This service contains the core application operations.
The controller is not responsible for checking duplicate email addresses.
The service returns DTOs instead of entities.
Database operations are wrapped in appropriate transaction boundaries.

package com.example.studentapi.common.exception; import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus; import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity; import org.springframework.web.bind.MethodArgumentNotValidException; import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ExceptionHandler; import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestControllerAdvice; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.Map; @RestControllerAdvice public class GlobalExceptionHandler { @ExceptionHandler(StudentNotFoundException.class) public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handleNotFound( StudentNotFoundException exception) { return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND) .body(new ApiError( "STUDENT_NOT_FOUND", exception.getMessage(), Map.of() )); } @ExceptionHandler(DuplicateEmailException.class) public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handleDuplicateEmail( DuplicateEmailException exception) { return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT) .body(new ApiError( "DUPLICATE_EMAIL", exception.getMessage(), Map.of() )); } @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class) public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handleValidation( MethodArgumentNotValidException exception) { Map<String, String> details = new LinkedHashMap<>(); exception.getBindingResult() .getFieldErrors() .forEach(error -> details.putIfAbsent( error.getField(), error.getDefaultMessage() ) ); return ResponseEntity.badRequest() .body(new ApiError( "VALIDATION_ERROR", "Request validation failed", details )); } }
This handler provides consistent responses for the expected application errors.
